chapter.title: The Exception Register
chapter.sub: Twelve exceptions on paper. Forty-one in the rooms. And the best rooms are breaking the standard.

items.text: SEASON 12 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT · CASE-060  Fenwright Group headquarters · month one · Maya (principal architect, one year), Rashida (CIO), Galen (senior technician), Noor (junior technician) and Teodor (head of EMEA) · Level L6 · Mastery support (reference only — choose the tool and say why)  Thirty offices, sixty meeting rooms, one standard — and a one-year contract whose last line reads: “Leave it so it doesn’t need you.” Maya starts by finding out what the rooms really are.  ⚑ RV-187: the CIO owns the standard and the change board; regional heads own their variants; each site owns its life safety. RV-188: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: The Exception Register
items.stakes: A standard with twelve exceptions on paper and forty-one in the rooms — and the best rooms are the ones breaking it.
items.clock: The CIO wants to know by Friday.
items.reward: Every difference owned and dated, the dangerous one with its owners — and the better way on its way into the standard.

objectives.text: Count what was never written down
Decide what happens to EMEA's rooms
Decide how exceptions live from now on

items.text: Cold open — “Nothing here should need you”
items.sub: Month one · Monday · 9:00 a.m. · Fenwright HQ

items.alt: Fenwright's architecture office: an estate board on the back wall shows thirty offices in three regions — AMERICAS, EMEA, APAC — every dot green; Rashida, the CIO, in a dark suit, gestures; Maya, new badge on her lanyard.

Then the first thing I need is to see what's really in the rooms.

items.prompt: Wednesday. Galen and Noor's scan is back: 41 of 60 rooms differ from the standard; the register lists 12. Your first move?
items.risk: Forcing back what works — or missing what's dangerous.
timeout: The scan sits in an inbox until the quarterly review.

hints.text: What do you need to know before you change anything?

options.label: Push the standard configuration to every non-conforming room tonight
options.result: Galen: “Including EMEA's? The only rooms nobody complains about?”

options.label: Read every difference with Galen and Noor: what, where, since when, why — and look for any that cross a safety or access boundary first
options.result: By Thursday lunch there's a list — and one line that stops the room: a fire-alarm mute input disabled in Singapore.

options.label: Rewrite the standard to match the rooms
options.result: The standard now includes a disabled fire-alarm input.

options.label: Send the scan to the regional heads and ask them to sort it out
options.result: Three regions, three spreadsheets, three answers.

items.title: Twelve on paper, forty-one in the rooms.
items.body: The register lists twelve exceptions. The rooms have forty-one differences: twenty-nine were never written down. Of the twelve that were, nine have no expiry date; the oldest ‘temporary’ one is six years old. And row three isn't a preference at all: a Singapore room's fire-alarm mute input — the one that silences the room when the alarm sounds — was disabled after nuisance mutes, ‘until refresh’. Nobody told the site's fire-alarm contractor.
items.label: Test: how many were never recorded — and how many never expire?

items.alt: A conformance scan drawn as sixty squares, one per room: 19 green (matches), 12 amber (recorded exceptions), 29 red (unrecorded differences) and one dark red square outlined — the disabled fire-alarm mute input. 41 of 60 rooms differ (68%); 9 of 12 recorded exceptions have no expiry.
items.caption: Forty-one.

items.title: ‘temporary — until refresh’
items.body: Row 3 of the old register, six years old: ‘Singapore 2: fire-alarm mute input disabled — nuisance mutes. Temporary, until refresh.’ There was no refresh. Nobody told the fire-alarm contractor.

items.title: Paved desire lines
items.body: Walk across any park and you'll find ‘desire lines’ — bare paths worn through the grass where people keep choosing a shorter way than the paved one. Some planners fence them off. Others wait a season, watch where the lines form, and pave those instead. A standard's exceptions are its desire lines. Some are shortcuts to be closed; some show you where the path should have been.

items.text: Act II — “The exception that was better”

items.title: The exception that was better.
items.body: Noor sorts the complaints by region and divides by rooms. EMEA: seven complaints from eighteen rooms last month — 0.39 per room. Everyone else: 1.2. The eighteen EMEA rooms all run the same unrecorded DSP template, with automatic mic mixing tuned for their glass-walled rooms. Teodor approved it for his region two years ago and never told the standard. It's an exception. It's also the best-performing configuration in the estate.
items.label: Test: compare the rates — and whose decision the standard is.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #112 · AVERY'S LENS  An exception is information, not a mistake  Every difference from the standard gets an owner, a reason, a risk and an expiry. Some go back to standard, some cross a boundary and go to their owner today — and some turn out to be better than the standard.  The register said twelve exceptions; the rooms had forty-one — and the best-performing rooms in the estate were the ones breaking the standard.

items.alt: A bar chart of complaints per room per month by region: AMERICAS 1.25 (25 from 20 rooms), EMEA 0.39 (7 from 18 rooms), APAC 1.14 (25 from 22 rooms). EMEA's unrecorded template draws about a third of the complaints per room.
items.caption: Rates, not totals.

items.prompt: Twenty-five years I've kept these rooms running. And now a register tells me I've been doing it wrong in forty-one of them.

options.label: “It tells me you kept them running. It doesn't tell me why — that's what I need from you.”
options.reply: …Now that I can do. Some of those twenty-nine have good reasons.

options.label: “The standard's the standard.”
options.reply: Then you'll find out which of your rooms nobody complains about.

options.label: “It's not personal.”
options.reply: It's my rooms. It's a bit personal.

items.prompt: EMEA's eighteen rooms break the standard — and work better than it. What do you recommend?
items.happening: EMEA's template: a third of the complaints.
unknown: How it behaves in other rooms
items.risk: Losing the best configuration in the estate — or spreading it untested.
timeout: The template stays a secret nobody can defend.

hints.text: Who owns the standard, and what would convince them?

options.label: Force them back to the standard — rules are rules
options.result: Complaints in EMEA triple within a month.

options.label: Record the template as a dated exception, test it in two AMERICAS rooms for a month, then take the evidence to Rashida's change board to promote it to the standard
options.result: Rashida: “Two rooms, one month, then I vote.” Teodor, for once, says nothing.
options.consequence: Promote with evidence, through the standard's owner.

options.label: Copy EMEA's template to all sixty rooms tonight
options.result: Glass-room tuning in carpeted rooms: the APAC low rooms start pumping.
options.consequence: The right idea without the test or the owner.

options.label: Leave it as an unrecorded regional quirk
options.result: Next year's architect forces it back.
options.consequence: Good work that nobody can find.

items.prompt: How do exceptions live from now on?
items.risk: Twenty-nine new unrecorded differences by next January.

hints.text: What turns a difference into a decision someone owns?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S12E01). Option B needs Documentation at LIMITED or better.

options.label: No exceptions at all — every room identical
options.result: The first 50 Hz office and the first glass room break it in a week.
options.consequence: A standard nobody can follow gets ignored.

options.label: One register in the standard: every exception with an owner, a reason, a risk and an expiry; life-safety and access issues to their owners the same day; a quarterly review in the CIO's calendar; anything that outperforms the standard goes to the change board
options.result: Rashida signs the register's first page. Forty-one rows, forty-one owners.
options.consequence: Recorded, owned, dated, reviewed — and a way to learn.

options.label: A shared spreadsheet the regional heads can edit
options.result: Three regions, three styles; half the rows have no dates by spring.
options.consequence: The best you can do without documentation discipline — a list, not a register.

options.label: Let each region keep its own list
options.result: Three lists, one standard, nobody sees the whole.

items.alt: The same sixty squares a week later: 20 green matching the standard (Singapore's input restored), 22 green owned and dated exceptions, 18 blue EMEA rooms in test for promotion. 41 of 41 differences owned, reasoned and dated; the fire-alarm mute input restored by its owners.
items.caption: Forty-one owners.

items.title: ‘EMEA-DSP-2 · T. approved’
items.body: The DSP template running in eighteen EMEA rooms: ‘EMEA-DSP-2 — automatic mixing tuned for glass rooms. Approved: T.’ Teodor approved it for his region. Nobody ever told the standard.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A standard and its rooms drift apart quietly. Before enforcing anything, read every difference: what, where, since when, why. Record each with an owner, a reason, a risk and an expiry; send anything that crosses a safety or access boundary to its owner the same day; compare rooms by rates, not totals; and when an exception works better than the standard, test it and take it to the standard's owner. Exceptions are information.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which ‘temporary’ fix in your work is older than a year?
